\chapter{Green and Yellow}
\label{ch:ta-green-and-yellow}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say green and yellow in Tamil, recognise \ta{பசுப்பு} as a rarer doublet, and keep the pan-Dravidian root separate from the independent one.}

Say \ta{பச்சை} as the pan-Dravidian green, \ta{மஞ்சள்} as a separate native yellow, and \ta{பசுப்பு} as the rarer doublet beside them.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ta{பச்சை}, \ta{மஞ்சள்}]{\ta{பச்சை}, \ta{மஞ்சள்} — closing the Dravidian arc, holding both patterns at once}

\label{lesson:TA-C22-paccai-manjal}



\begin{quote}
You've now seen three different Dravidian answers to \textquotedblleft{}how do green and yellow relate\textquotedblright{}: Kannada split them apart, Telugu fused them into one root, Malayalam kept them as two separate native words. Tamil, it turns out, quietly contains a trace of \textbf{both} of the last two patterns.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{பச்சை} — the familiar pan-Dravidian green}
\textbf{\ta{பச்சை}} (\textbf{paccai}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{green}\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ \textbf{Proto-Dravidian} \emph{\textbf{*pac-}} — the same root you've now met four times: Kannada's \emph{hasiru}, Telugu's \emph{pacca}, Malayalam's \emph{paccha}, and now Tamil's own \emph{paccai}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{மஞ்சள்}} (\textbf{mañcaḷ}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{yellow, turmeric}\textquotedblright{}) is Tamil's actual, everyday word for yellow — and it comes from a \textbf{completely separate} native Dravidian root, matching Malayalam's \textbf{\ml{മഞ്ഞ}/\ml{മഞ്ഞൾ}} (\emph{mañña}/\emph{maññaḷ}) closely. Like Malayalam's pair, this root has no Sanskrit involvement — it sits alongside \emph{paccai}, not descended from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
The \textbf{Tamil Lexicon} also records \textbf{\ta{பசுப்பு}} (\textbf{pacuppu}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{greenish yellow}\textquotedblright{}) — a genuine \textbf{doublet} of \emph{paccai} itself, from the same \emph{\textbf{*pac-}} root, matching Telugu's \emph{pasupu} closely. Unlike Telugu, though, this doublet is \textbf{not} Tamil's everyday word for yellow — that job belongs to \emph{mañcaḷ}; \emph{pacuppu} survives mainly as a dictionary-recorded shade word. So Tamil alone holds a trace of \textbf{both} patterns at once: a \emph{pac-} doublet sitting quietly in the dictionary (Telugu's pattern), next to a separate, dominant root doing the everyday work (Malayalam's pattern).

(Note for the Tamil-speaking reviewer: \emph{pacuppu}'s everyday currency is the part I'm least certain of — please confirm whether it's a word you'd recognize as \textquotedblleft{}greenish yellow,\textquotedblright{} or whether it reads as archaic/purely literary in the Tamil you'd teach first.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ta{பச்சை}\textquotedblright{} — green, the pan-Dravidian \emph{pac- word}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ta{மஞ்சள்}\textquotedblright{} — yellow, Tamil's real everyday word, a separate root
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ta{பசுப்பு}\textquotedblright{} — a rarer doublet of paccai, echoing Telugu's pattern
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is Tamil's everyday word for yellow, and is it related to \textbf{paccai}? (\textbf{\ta{மஞ்சள்}}, \emph{mañcaḷ} — \textbf{no}, a completely separate native root, matching Malayalam's \emph{mañña/maññaḷ}.) What rarer Tamil word IS a doublet of \emph{paccai}, from the same \emph{pac-} root? (\textbf{\ta{பசுப்பு}}, \emph{pacuppu}, \textquotedblleft{}greenish yellow\textquotedblright{} — echoing Telugu's \emph{pacca/pasupu} pattern.) Does any one pattern hold across all four major Dravidian languages? (\textbf{No} — Kannada splits native/loan, Telugu fuses one root, Malayalam keeps two separate roots, and Tamil turns out to hold traces of both Telugu's and Malayalam's patterns at once.)
\end{tcolorbox}
